Further studies and demonstrations are needed to understand the compatibility of alternative fuels with existing locomotive engines and to provide emissions factors for these types of studies. Additional research is needed on developing advanced engine technologies such as dual-fuel systems and retrofitting options while maintaining performance and emissions standards. 7.3 FUEL BLENDS AND OPTIMIZATION Exploring and demonstrating optimal fuel blends that balance environmental benefits with operational feasibility is essential. Research should investigate the effects of different biofuel blends on engine performance, emissions, and maintenance requirements. This includes studying 63 the long-term impacts of using BD blends, RD, and other non-drop-in fuels in various locomotive configurations. 7.4 TECHNOECONOMIC ANALYSIS (TEA) Among the 16 selected alternative fuel pathways, biocrude from sewage sludge HTL has the lowest estimated MFSP without incentives. However, it cannot be directly used as a drop-in fuel for existing locomotive engines. The estimated MFSP of all pathways producing RD, a drop-in fuel, ranges from $3.47 to $4.65 per DGE without incentives. Existing incentive programs may further decrease the estimated MFSP and improve the economic feasibility of alternative fuel production. Note that the TEA conducted in this work was based on standardized economic assumption for a Nth-plant application, which are subject to several uncertainties. An "Nth-plant" refers to a chemical plant that replicates a design already validated by prior operations, thereby typically offering reduced risks and capital costs compared to a first-of-a-kind facility. A detailed business case study is crucial to thoroughly assess whether producing alternative fuels is economically viable in a specific region or project. This study should consider the unique characteristics of local feedstocks and various financial projections. Furthermore, the analysis should incorporate key economic indicators like net present value, internal rate of return, and payback period, because these provide a more practical perspective for industrial adoption. For technologies that are still in the early to mid-stages of development (low- to mid-level TRLs), the TEA should be regularly revised to reflect improvements in performance over time and to minimize uncertainties. 7.5 LIFECYCLE AND ENVIRONMENTAL IMPACT ASSESSMENTS Most of the renewable fuel options could provide 80% CO e emission reduction, compared to the 2 conventional diesel used in the freight rail sector. Future studies can look into other agricultural waste feedstocks such as cotton stalk or other oilseed feedstocks such as carinata, camelina, and canola. While WTP lifecycle SO emissions are estimated and presented in this study, a significant X knowledge gap remains in the pump-to-wheel SO emissions. X Future research should focus on estimating combustion related emissions of both carbon dioxide and CAPs for more robust lifecycle assessment results. In other words, comprehensive lifecycle assessments should be validated with demonstrations to confirm the environmental impacts of alternative fuels across their entire supply chain. 7.6 FEEDSTOCK AVAILABILITY AND SUPPLY CHAIN LOGISTICS The biomass resource data from the DOE 2023 Billion Ton study (DOE, 2024) was used to provide insights into the supply curves (availability and cost) of feedstocks to produce the alternative fuels studied here.
